source.heading: PASSAGE A
source.directions: Read the following passage and answer the questions that follow.

passage.text: Returning home after a decade and half abroad, our Geography master remained incurably addicted to foreign ways and ideas for years after landing here.
He would forever stick to his theory of Africans suffering from a curse inflicted on them by the Almighty God for some heinous sins committed centuries ago.
He would, in support of this theory, ask listeners: "Why would our mosquito inflict deadly malaria on us whereas the British mosquito does not bite?
Why aren't there poisonous snakes in Britain whereas here most snakes are deadly?
Why should the deadly sickle cell disease be peculiar to the black race?"
Of course, he hardly waits for answers to these and similar questions before jumping to the same inevitable conclusion.
However, he met his match one day when a new student joined the class and heard the litany we were used to.
The new boy calmly said, "Sir, I happen to know a few white men who suffer from the sickle cell disease; some are Italians and some are Spanish.
The mosquito is equally deadly in India, South-east Asian Countries and South America.
The United States and some other South American Countries have their deadly snakes.
And, Sir, I know many white men, some of them British, who would prefer our brilliant sunshine to their horribly cold winter."
I had never, before that day, seen our master so consumed with anger.
He directed a burning look at the poor boy, who had no answer to this new battle.
Without as much as saying a single word, the master stalked out of the classroom.
Needless to say, our anger was turned on the new boy, who had decided to rock the boat without taking the time to sound the water.
A delegation was sent to the master to apologise to him.
But we all noticed something rather unusual thereafter never again did he dwell on the issue of Africans being the cursed People.

questions.stem: What point of view is the Geography master fond of advancing?

options.text: Africans are infested with all kinds of problem
options.why: This is too general. It leaves out his explanation for the problems.

options.text: Only the white men are free from deadly diseases
options.why: The master gives examples to back a wider claim about a curse.

options.text: The Almighty God is punishing Africans for sins they committed long ago.
options.why: Sentence 2 gives the master's theory directly.

options.text: God did not curse the white people.
options.why: This leaves out what the master says happened to Africans and why.

questions.stem: Which of the following arguments did he not use to support his vies?

options.text: In Africa, the mosquito causes deadly malaria whereas in Britain, it doesn't bite or caw e malaria
options.why: Sentence 3 shows he contrasts the African and British mosquitoes.

options.text: There is malaria both in Britain and in African Countries
options.why: The master claims the British mosquito does not bite. He does not say both places have malaria.

options.text: The snakes in Africa are deadly but those in Britain are harmless
options.why: Sentence 4 shows he relies on a contrast between snakes in the two places.

options.text: The sickle cell disease is peculiar to the black race.
options.why: Sentence 5 shows he treats sickle cell disease as peculiar to one group.

questions.stem: "...rock the boat" What figure of speech is this expression?

options.text: Simile
options.why: It does not make a comparison using words such as like or as.

options.text: Metaphor
options.why: The boy upset the usual order in class. The boat stands for that situation.

options.text: Personification
options.why: The expression does not give a thing human qualities.

options.text: Hyperbole
options.why: The expression makes an indirect comparison. It is not an exaggeration.

questions.stem: What extra argument (lid the new boy offer after countering each of vie master's points?

options.text: There are problems especially in Africa
options.why: He gives examples outside Africa. This is not his extra point.

options.text: There are deadly snakes be the in America and Africa
options.why: Deadly snakes are part of his reply to the teacher's earlier claims.

options.text: There are harmless snakes in Britain
options.why: He answers the snake claim with examples from the Americas.

options.text: Many white men prefer the African climate to their own.
options.why: After the replies about disease and snakes, he describes people who prefer the sunshine.

questions.stem: Why do you think the master fought back with his look rather than with further argument?

options.text: He knew that the boy's points were valid
options.why: The student gives counterexamples. The master leaves without replying and does not repeat the claim.

options.text: He had answers to the boy's argument
options.why: The passage shows him looking angry and leaving without an answer.

options.text: He went out to sort for the boy's argument
options.why: The passage gives no sign that he left to look for a reply.

options.text: He already made up his mind on his points.
options.why: The master had a firm view earlier. That alone misses why he stops defending it after this exchange.
